title: With all his might (2 Samuel 6:14–16)
hookLine: the king dances before the ark; Michal despises it

cards: Shouting. The blast of the shofar. A crowd pressing up the road into Jerusalem, and in the middle of it the ark of the covenant, carried up into the city.
David is king now. He could ride beside it in robes, nodding to the crowd. Instead he's out in front of it, in the dust, dancing.
Not a polite sway: the kind of dancing that makes people stare. And above the street, at a window, someone is watching. The same woman who once lowered him through a window to save his life.

teach.b: Here's the verse: "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod." With all his might: in Hebrew, b'chol oz, with all strength. Nothing held back for his dignity.

And he's not in the king's robes but a linen ephod, a simple garment the text gives to priests and to the boy Samuel serving at the shrine. Some translators render the dancing as whirling; the next verses add leaping.
Then the camera moves to the window.
Michal, the daughter of Saul, sees King David leaping and dancing before the Lord, and despises him in her heart.
Notice how she's named: not David's wife, but the daughter of Saul, as if the old house is looking down at the new.
When David comes home she meets him with sarcasm: how the king of Israel honored himself today, uncovering himself before the servants' maids.
David answers that it was before the Lord he danced, and he'll be humbler still. Some readers hold this up as joy in God that doesn't stop to ask how it looks. Others make room for Michal's side.

The woman at the first window gave everything for David. Between the two windows, the book has told us, Saul gave her to another man, and David later had her taken back while that husband walked behind her, weeping.
It shows a king who forgot himself, and a woman who couldn't.

how: Jews read David's dance before the ark in the book of Samuel, part of the Prophets, and dancing with joy in worship carries on in Jewish life, as when people dance with the Torah scrolls on Simchat Torah.

o: with great dignity, as befits a king
with all strength, holding nothing back
with quiet reverence, head bowed low

games.q: with all his might — tap the pairs.
p: how the text names Michal here

s: David danced in his royal robes
he was girded with a linen ephod, a simple garment.
Michal despised David in her heart
she saw him leaping and dancing before the Lord, and despised him.
David apologized to Michal for dancing

games.q: you're David, king of Israel, walking in front of the ark as it comes into your city. the whole crowd is watching. what do you do?
o: walk beside it with royal dignity.
dance before it with all your might.
let the priests lead and watch from a window.
games.why: he danced before the Lord with all his might, in a linen ephod, leaping and whirling in the road.

practice: If you're somewhere private, stand; if not, or you can't stand, you can do this sitting: shoulders, hands, head.
Put on a song, in your head or out loud, something that makes you glad, and move to it with all your might, not well and not for anyone. If you pray, you can let the movement be your prayer.

wordCard.voice: b'chol oz. The Hebrew for with all strength, how David danced before the ark in a linen garment, holding nothing back. Today's word.
